Illposedness for dispersive equations:
Degenerate dispersion and Takeuchi–Mizohata condition

In-Jee Jeong ††thanks: Department of Mathematical Sciences and Research Institute of Mathematics, Seoul National University.
E-mail: injee_j@snu.ac.kr    Sung-Jin Oh ††thanks: Department of Mathematics, UC Berkeley and School of Mathematics, Korea Institute for Advanced Study. E-mail: sjoh@math.berkeley.edu
August 24, 2026
Abstract

We provide a unified viewpoint on two illposedness mechanisms for dispersive equations in one spatial dimension, namely degenerate dispersion and (the failure of) the Takeuchi–Mizohata condition. Our approach is based on a robust energy- and duality-based method introduced in an earlier work of the authors in the setting of Hall-magnetohydynamics. Concretely, the main results in this paper concern strong illposedness of the Cauchy problem (e.g., non-existence and unboundedness of the solution map) in high-regularity Sobolev spaces for various quasilinear degenerate Schrödinger- and KdV-type equations, including the Hunter–Smothers equation, K⁡(m,n)K(m,n) models of Rosenau–Hyman, and the inviscid surface growth model. The mechanism behind these results may be understood in terms of combination of two effects: degenerate dispersion – which is a property of the principal term in the presence of degenerating coefficients – and the evolution of the amplitude governed by the Takeuchi–Mizohata condition – which concerns the subprincipal term. We also demonstrate how the same techniques yield a more quantitative version of the classical L2L^{2}-illposedness result by Mizohata for linear variable-coefficient Schrödinger equations with failed Takeuchi–Mizohata condition.

1 Introduction

1.1 Quasilinear degenerate dispersive equations

In this paper, we study the issue of illposedness of the Cauchy problem for various quasilinear dispersive equations in one spatial dimension in the presence of degenerate dispersion. We consider both Schrödinger and KdV-type equations. Examples of Schrödinger-type equations we treat include, for instance, the Hunter–Smothers equation [15]

i​∂tϕ+∂x(|ϕ|2​∂xϕ)=0,\displaystyle i\partial_{t}\phi+\partial_{x}(|\phi|^{2}\partial_{x}\phi)=0, (1.1)

which was derived from the Majda–Rosales–Schonbeck equation [20] describing the resonant reflection of sound waves off a sawtooth entropy wave, as well as its Hamiltonian variant considered by Germain, Harrop-Griffith and Marzuola [11, 14]

i​∂tϕ+ϕ¯​∂x(ϕ​∂xϕ)−μ0​|ϕ|2​ϕ=0(μ0=−1,0,1),i\partial_{t}\phi+\overline{\phi}\partial_{x}(\phi\partial_{x}\phi)-\mu_{0}|{\phi}|^{2}\phi=0\qquad(\mu_{0}=-1,0,1), (1.2)

where ϕ:ℝ+×𝕋→ℂ\phi:\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\mathbb{T}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}. In the KdV case, our results cover the K⁡(m,n)K(m,n) equation of Rosenau–Hyman [30] with n=2n=2, i.e.,

∂tu+(1m​um)x+(12​u2)x​x​x=0(m​ is a nonnegative integer),\partial_{t}u+(\tfrac{1}{m}u^{m})_{x}+(\tfrac{1}{2}u^{2})_{xxx}=0\quad(m\hbox{ is a nonnegative integer}), (1.3)

which has been studied extensively in connection with the remarkable nonlinear phenomenon of the existence of compactons (solitons with compact spatial support) [27, 28, 29, 30, 35, 36] (see [31] for a recent review), as well as the inviscid surface growth model (see [6, 7, 8, 26] for the full surface growth model, with the dissipation −ν​hx​x​x​x-\nu h_{xxxx} on the right-hand side)

∂th+((hx)2)x​x=0,\partial_{t}h+((h_{x})^{2})_{xx}=0, (1.4)

where u,h:ℝ+×𝕋→ℝu,h:\mathbb{R}_{+}\times\mathbb{T}\to\mathbb{R}. Indeed, degenerate KdV-type equations similar in form to (1.3) appear in various subjects including sedimentation models ([37, 5]), shoreline problem in water waves ([19]) and magma dynamics ([32, 33]), to name a few. A more extensive list of references on degenerate KdV equations can be found in [11, 10].

In each of these equations, observe that the the highest order term is nonlinear – more specifically, quadratic or cubic – in the solution. Vanishing of the solution, therefore, leads to some kind of “degeneracy” of the highest order term, which in turn gives rise to delicate issues in the (local) well-posedness of the associated Cauchy problem.

Indeed, for initial data that are uniformly bounded away from 00 (a property henceforth referred to as nondegeneracy), one expects local well-posedness in high-regularity L2L^{2}-based Sobolev spaces Hs​(𝕋)H^{s}(\mathbb{T}). For example, in the case of (1.1), for a sufficiently regular solution ϕ\phi, one has the conservation of the L2L^{2}-norm:

dd​t​(∫𝕋|ϕ|2​𝑑x)=0.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(\int_{\mathbb{T}}|\phi|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x\right)=0.

Obtaining higher regularity apriori estimates is a much more nontrivial task. One can observe the following bound for n≥1n\geq 1 (in operator notation) at each tt:

dd​t(∫𝕋|(∂x|ϕ|2∂x)nϕ|2dx)≲n∥ϕ∥H2​n4​n+2.\begin{split}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(\int_{\mathbb{T}}|(\partial_{x}|\phi|^{2}\partial_{x})^{n}\phi|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x\right)\lesssim_{n}\|{\phi}\|_{H^{2n}}^{4n+2}.\end{split}

Furthermore, as long as the solution stays nondegenerate at tt, in the sense that infx|ϕ⁡(x,t)|2>c\inf_{x}|\phi(x,t)|^{2}>c for some c>0c>0, a standard argument involving the ellipticity of (∂x|ϕ(x,t)|2∂x)n(\partial_{x}|\phi(x,t)|^{2}\partial_{x})^{n} allows us to bound ‖ϕ⁡(⋅,t)‖H2​n2\|{\phi(\cdot,t)}\|_{H^{2n}}^{2} by the integral on the left-hand side up to errors of the form O⁡(‖ϕ⁡(⋅,t)‖H2​n4​n+2)O(\|{\phi(\cdot,t)}\|_{H^{2n}}^{4n+2}). Putting these together, one can establish a short-time H2​nH^{2n} apriori estimate for the solution ϕ\phi with nondegenerate initial data. However, in the case of degenerate initial data (i.e., those without a uniform bound away from 00), the above scheme for a short-time H2​nH^{2n} apriori estimate with n≥1n\geq 1 clearly breaks down.

In this paper, we show that this failure of proof of higher derivative apriori estimates is, in fact, a manifestation of genuine illposedness in standard function spaces. Despite the formal conservation of the L2L^{2}-norm, we demonstrate that all of the equations above are rather strongly ill-posed – in the sense of non-existence of solutions and unboundedness of the data-to-solution map in suitable set-ups – in a neighborhood of degenerate initial data (e.g., zero data) in high-regularity spaces (Ck−1,1C^{k-1,1}, Sobolev or Hölder spaces).

1.2 Main results for quasilinear degenerate dispersive equations

1.2.1 Results for Schrödinger-type equations

To treat the Hunter–Smothers equation (1.1) and the Hamiltonian equation (1.2) simultaneously, we shall consider the general equation

i​∂tϕ+|ϕ|2​∂x​xϕ+α1​ϕ​|∂xϕ|2+β1​ϕ¯​(∂xϕ)2+μ1​|ϕ|2​ϕ=0,i\partial_{t}\phi+|{\phi}|^{2}\partial_{xx}\phi+\alpha_{1}\phi|{\partial_{x}\phi}|^{2}+\beta_{1}\overline{\phi}(\partial_{x}\phi)^{2}+\mu_{1}|{\phi}|^{2}\phi=0, (1.5)

where ϕ:ℝt×ℝx→ℂ\phi:\mathbb{R}_{t}\times\mathbb{R}_{x}\to\mathbb{C}, α1,β1∈ℝ\alpha_{1},\beta_{1}\in\mathbb{R} and μ1∈ℂ\mu_{1}\in\mathbb{C}. Indeed, the case α1=β1=1\alpha_{1}=\beta_{1}=1 and μ1=0\mu_{1}=0 corresponds to (1.1), while the case α1=0\alpha_{1}=0 and β1=1\beta_{1}=1 corresponds to (1.2).

For the statement of the main results, we need to introduce the following exponents. Given α1,β1∈ℝ\alpha_{1},\beta_{1}\in\mathbb{R}, we introduce the exponent

σc=−(α12+β1−1),\sigma_{c}=-(\frac{\alpha_{1}}{2}+\beta_{1}-1), (1.6)

and let scs_{c} be the smallest integer greater than 11 and σc−12\sigma_{c}-\frac{1}{2}, i.e.,

sc=max⁡{2,⌊σc−12⌋+1}.s_{c}=\max\{2,\lfloor\sigma_{c}-\tfrac{1}{2}\rfloor+1\}. (1.7)

Note that σc=−12\sigma_{c}=-\frac{1}{2} and sc=2s_{c}=2 for (1.1), while σc=0\sigma_{c}=0 and sc=2s_{c}=2 for (1.2). For the significance of σc\sigma_{c} and ⌊σc−12⌋+1\lfloor\sigma_{c}-\tfrac{1}{2}\rfloor+1, see Remark 1.3 and Section 1.3. We note already that the lower bound sc≥2s_{c}\geq 2 is a technical byproduct of our proof, which we have not attempted to optimize.

Our first result is unboundedness of the solution map (i.e., norm inflation) in CscC^{s_{c}} near any solution with a linear degeneracy.

Theorem 1.1 (Unboundedness of the solution map near a linearly degenerate solution).

Assume that there exists a solution f∈L∞​([0,δ],Csc+1,1​(𝕋))f\in L^{\infty}([0,\delta];C^{s_{c}+1,1}(\mathbb{T})) to (1.5) with some δ>0\delta>0 such that f⁡(t=0)=f0f(t=0)=f_{0} is linearly degenerate; that is, there exists x0∈𝕋x_{0}\in\mathbb{T} with f⁡(x0)=0f(x_{0})=0 and f0′​(x0)≠0f_{0}^{\prime}(x_{0})\neq 0.

Then, for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0, s0≥scs_{0}\geq s_{c}, and 0<δ′≤δ0<\delta^{\prime}\leq\delta, we can find ϕ~0∈C∞​(𝕋)\widetilde{\phi}_{0}\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}) such that ‖ϕ~0‖Cs0≤ϵ\|{\widetilde{\phi}_{0}}\|_{C^{s_{0}}}\leq\epsilon and one of the following holds:

  • •

    there exists no L∞​([0,δ′],Csc​(𝕋))L^{\infty}([0,\delta^{\prime}];C^{s_{c}}(\mathbb{T})) solution to (1.5) with initial data f0+ϕ~0f_{0}+\widetilde{\phi}_{0}; or

  • •

    any L∞​([0,δ′],Csc​(𝕋))L^{\infty}([0,\delta^{\prime}];C^{s_{c}}(\mathbb{T})) solution ϕ\phi with ϕ⁡(t=0)=f0+ϕ~0\phi(t=0)=f_{0}+\widetilde{\phi}_{0} satisfies

    sup0<t<δ′‖ϕ⁡(t,⋅)−f⁡(t,⋅)‖Csc​(𝕋)>c0​(δ′)−12,\begin{split}\sup_{0<t<\delta^{\prime}}\|{\phi(t,\cdot)-f(t,\cdot)}\|_{C^{s_{c}}(\mathbb{T})}>c_{0}(\delta^{\prime})^{-\frac{1}{2}},\end{split}

    with some c0>0c_{0}>0 depending only on ff.

We remark that the norm inflation assertion immediately implies the inflation of any norm that controls CscC^{s_{c}}, such as HσH^{\sigma} with σ>sc+12\sigma>s_{c}+\frac{1}{2}. In fact, our proof readily extends to norm inflation in HσH^{\sigma} for any σ>σc\sigma>\sigma_{c} in the second alternative, which is expected to be sharp according to Remark 1.3 and Section 1.3 below; see Remark 2.10 for further details. We also remark that the statement of Theorem 1.1 should extend over to the case of solutions with orders of degeneracy other than 1. For simplicity, however, we restrict ourselves to the linearly degenerate case, which is “critical” in some sense; see Section 1.3 below.

Our second result is the nonexistence of a regular local-in-time solution in arbitrarily high-regularity Cs0C^{s_{0}} spaces.

Theorem 1.2 (Nonexistence of regular local-in-time solution).

For any ϵ>0\epsilon>0 and s0≥sc+2s_{0}\geq s_{c}+2, there exists an initial data ϕ0∈C∞​(𝕋)\phi_{0}\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}) satisfying ‖ϕ0‖Cs0<ϵ\|{\phi_{0}}\|_{C^{s_{0}}}<\epsilon for which there is no corresponding solution to (1.5) belonging to L∞​([0,δ],Csc+2​(𝕋))L^{\infty}([0,\delta];{C}^{s_{c}+2}(\mathbb{T})) with any δ>0\delta>0.

As an immediate corollary of the above, we have that (1.1) and (1.2) are ill-posed in the strongest sense of Hadamard in function spaces which contains C∞C^{\infty} and controls the C4C^{4}–norm (where 4=sc+24=s_{c}+2): there exists C∞C^{\infty} initial data without a local solution in Lt∞​Ws,pL^{\infty}_{t}W^{s,p} with s−1p>4s-\frac{1}{p}>4 and Lt∞​Ck,αL^{\infty}_{t}C^{k,\alpha} with k+α≥4k+\alpha\geq 4.

Remark 1.3 (Exponents σc\sigma_{c}, scs_{c}, Takeuchi–Mizohata condition and degenerate dispersion).

Observe that the illposedness results, Theorems 1.1–1.2, hold for all possible coefficients α1\alpha_{1}, β1\beta_{1} in front of subprincipal terms, although these possibly alter the exponents σc\sigma_{c} and scs_{c}. Heuristically, σc\sigma_{c} is the expected critical L2L^{2}-Sobolev regularity exponent above which the linearization of (1.5) around a regular linearly degenerate solution is ill-posed. In fact, the negativity of σc\sigma_{c} already signals L2L^{2}-illposedness of the linearized equation by the classical Takeuchi–Mizohata condition [25, Chapter VII]! Even if σc\sigma_{c} is positive, it turns out to be L∞L^{\infty}-ill-posed after taking kk many derivatives with k>σc−12k>\sigma_{c}-\frac{1}{2}. This consideration motivates the exponent scs_{c} and our illposedness results. We shall elaborate on this remark in Section 1.3.

1.2.2 Results for KdV-type equations

To unify our treatment of KdV-type equations, we consider the general equation

∂tu+u​ux​x​x+α1​ux​ux​x+μ1m​(um)x=0,\partial_{t}u+uu_{xxx}+\alpha_{1}u_{x}u_{xx}+\frac{\mu_{1}}{m}(u^{m})_{x}=0, (1.8)

where u:ℝt×ℝx→ℝu:\mathbb{R}_{t}\times\mathbb{R}_{x}\to\mathbb{R}, α1∈ℝ\alpha_{1}\in\mathbb{R}, μ1∈ℝ\mu_{1}\in\mathbb{R} and mm is an integer greater than or equal to 22. Note that there is no need to separately consider the case m=1m=1, as then this term can be easily removed by the change of variables (t,x)=(t′,x′+μ1​t′)(t,x)=(t^{\prime},x^{\prime}+\mu_{1}t^{\prime}).

Note that α1=3\alpha_{1}=3 and μ1=1\mu_{1}=1 corresponds to the K⁡(m,2)K(m,2) equation (1.3). The inviscid surface growth model (1.4) reduces to the case α1=3\alpha_{1}=3 and μ1=0\mu_{1}=0 after making the change of variables u=2​hxu=\sqrt{2}h_{x}.

In the present case, the role of linear degeneracy in the Schrödinger case is played by cubic degeneracy, see Section 1.3, below. As before, we introduce the constant

σc=−(α1−32),\sigma_{c}=-(\alpha_{1}-\frac{3}{2}),

and the regularity exponent

sc=max⁡{5,⌊σc−12⌋+1}.s_{c}=\max\{5,\lfloor\sigma_{c}-\tfrac{1}{2}\rfloor+1\}.

Here, σc\sigma_{c} is the critical L2L^{2}-Sobolev regularity exponent above which the linearization of (1.8) around a regular cubically degenerate solution is ill-posed (see Section 1.3 below). The linearized equation is L∞L^{\infty}-ill-posed after taking kk many derivatives with k>σc−12k>\sigma_{c}-\frac{1}{2}; this motivates the exponent scs_{c}. The lower bound sc≥5s_{c}\geq 5 is again a nonoptimal technical byproduct of our proof; see Proposition 3.2 for where it is used.

Theorem 1.4 (Unboundedness of the solution map near a cubically degenerate solution).

Assume that there exists a solution f∈L∞​([0,δ],Cs−1,1​(I))f\in L^{\infty}([0,\delta];C^{s-1,1}(I)) of (1.8) with some δ>0\delta>0 and I=[a,b]I=[a,b], such that the initial data f0f_{0} is positive on I∖∂II\setminus\partial I, vanishes cubically on ∂I\partial I and f0∈Cs0−1,1f_{0}\in C^{s_{0}-1,1}, where sc≤s≤s0s_{c}\leq s\leq s_{0}.     there exists no solution to (1.8) with initial data f0+ϕ0f_{0}+\phi_{0} that belongs to L∞​([0,δ′],Cs−1,1​(I))L^{\infty}([0,\delta^{\prime}];C^{s-1,1}(I)); or

  • •

    any solution uu with u⁡(0)=f0+ϕ0u(0)=f_{0}+\phi_{0} and belonging to L∞​([0,δ′],Cs−1,1​(I))L^{\infty}([0,\delta^{\prime}];C^{s-1,1}(I)) satisfies, for every sc≤s′≤2​⌊s2⌋s_{c}\leq s^{\prime}\leq 2\lfloor\frac{s}{2}\rfloor,

    sup0<t<δ′‖u⁡(t,⋅)−f⁡(t,⋅)‖Cs′​(I)>(δ′)−12.\sup_{0<t<\delta^{\prime}}\|{u(t,\cdot)-f(t,\cdot)}\|_{C^{s^{\prime}}(I)}>(\delta^{\prime})^{-\frac{1}{2}}.

The nonexistence result for (1.8) is as follows.

Theorem 1.5 (Nonexistence of regular local-in-time solution).

For any ϵ>0\epsilon>0 and sc≤s≤s0s_{c}\leq s\leq s_{0}, where ss is an even integer, there exist an initial data u0∈C∞​(𝕋)u_{0}\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}) satisfying ‖u0‖Cs0<ϵ\|{u_{0}}\|_{C^{s_{0}}}<\epsilon for which there is no corresponding solution to (1.8) belonging to L∞​([0,δ],Cs​(𝕋))L^{\infty}([0,\delta];C^{s}(\mathbb{T})) for any δ>0\delta>0.

Remark 1.6.

We now give a few simple remarks regarding the above.

  • •

    In all of the above, the physical domain could be taken to be ℝ\mathbb{R} instead of 𝕋\mathbb{T}.

  • •

    Our proof easily extends to norm inflation in HσH^{\sigma} for any σ>σc\sigma>\sigma_{c} in the second alternative in Theorem 1.4. Moreover, in contrast to the Schödinger case, we may also easily extend Theorem 1.5 to the non-existence of solutions in HσH^{\sigma} for any σ>max⁡{σc,5+12}\sigma>\max\{\sigma_{c},5+\frac{1}{2}\} (see Remark 1.14 for why the situations are different). These numerologies are expected to be sharp, as we shall discuss in Section 1.3 below. We refer the reader to Remark 2.10 for more details on this modification (which is for norm inflation in the Schrödinger case, but the overall idea is the same).

  • •

    As one can expect, the lower order term (um)x(u^{m})_{x}, for any m≥2m\geq 2, does not play any essential role in the proof of illposedness of (1.8). Similarly, one can treat versions of (1.1) which have some lower order terms.

  • •

    We expect our results to generalize to K⁡(m,n)K(m,n) with n>2n>2, as well as 𝒞⁡(m,a,b)\mathcal{C}(m,a,b) equations [29] with n:=a+b>2n:=a+b>2, by considering degeneracies of order 3n−1\frac{3}{n-1} (which are critical).

Remark 1.7 (Comparison with the work of Ambrose–Simpson–Wright–Yang [3]).

In the pioneering paper [3], the illposedness of ut=u​ux​x​xu_{t}=uu_{xxx} in the (fairly low regularity) Sobolev space H2H^{2} has been proved based on the construction of a compactly supported H2H^{2} (but not smooth) self-similar solution AA. However, the existence of such a solution is specific to the equation ut=u​ux​x​xu_{t}=uu_{xxx}, and the proof does not extend to more general class of equations (1.8), nor to higher regularity Sobolev spaces, as in our results. Our approach is distinct from that of [3]: it does not involve self-similar solutions, but is rather based on appropriate smooth wave packet-type approximate solutions traveling towards the degeneracy; see Section 1.3 below. While our results (Theorems 1.4 and 1.5) do not cover Sobolev regularities as low as H2H^{2} due to technical reasons, our heuristics suggest that our illposedness mechanism should extend to HσH^{\sigma} with σ>σc=32\sigma>\sigma_{c}=\frac{3}{2}.

Nevertheless, we point out that a key heuristic consideration of our approach, namely, the combined effect of degenerate dispersion and sub-principal term, can already be found in [3], albeit with a different viewpoint.

Remark 1.8 (Comparison with the works of Germain–Harrop-Griffith–Marzuola [10] and Harrop-Griffith–Marzuola [14]).

For solutions to (1.1) and (1.2) with degenerate initial data (i.e., initial data with a zero), our proof identifies and exploits, in a nonlinear fashion, a mechanism by which energies in low frequencies are transferred to high frequencies at arbitrarily fast rates, where the frequencies are defined with respect to the original variable xx. We emphasize, however, that it does not rule out the possibility of well-posedness in regularity classes adapted to the degeneracies of the initial data, by working with a renormalized variable and/or suitable weights. Indeed, such positive results have been proved in the interesting works of Germain–Harrop-Griffith–Marzuola for a KdV-type quasilinear dispersive equation [10], and Harrop-Griffith–Marzuola for (1.2) [14], where Lagrangian-type coordinates adapted to the solution were used to formulate the function spaces.

1.3 Key mechanism: degenerate dispersion and Takeuchi–Mizohata condition

The nonlinear illposedness results in this paper are firmly based on a detailed and quantitative understanding of illposedness for the linearized equation around a background solution ff whose initial data contains a degeneracy. For simplicity, in this subsection we shall assume that the linearization takes the form

{∂tu−i​∂x(a​∂xu)−i​b​∂xu=(lower order) in the Schrödinger case,∂tu+12​(∂x3(a​u)+a​∂x3u)+b​∂x2u=(lower order) in the KdV case,\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u-i\partial_{x}(a\partial_{x}u)-ib\partial_{x}u=(\hbox{lower order})&\hbox{ in the Schr\"{o}dinger case},\\ \partial_{t}u+\tfrac{1}{2}(\partial_{x}^{3}(au)+a\partial_{x}^{3}u)+b\partial_{x}^{2}u=(\hbox{lower order})&\hbox{ in the KdV case},\end{cases} (1.9)

where a=a⁡(x)a=a(x) is real-valued in both cases, and b=b⁡(x)b=b(x) is also real-valued in the KdV case.11 1 For Schrödinger-type problems, we regard first-order terms of the form b~​(x)​∂xu¯\widetilde{b}(x)\partial_{x}\overline{u} as (lower order), as it can be removed by a suitable change of the dependent variable; see the introduction of ψ\psi in §2.3.2 below.

Remark 1.9 (On time independence of the coefficients in (1.9)).

While we assumed that a⁡(x)a(x) and b⁡(x)b(x) are time independent, the actual linearization of (1.5) and (1.8) on a dynamic background solution f⁡(t,x)f(t,x) would, of course, have time-dependent coefficients. Nevertheless, the time scale of the illposedness mechanism is arbitrarily short, and hence we may effectively approximate these coefficients by the initial values for the purpose of our discussion.

It is conceptually useful to distinguish two intertwined mechanisms for illposedness, degenerate dispersion and Takeuchi–Mizohata instability, which can be seen from the principal and sub-principal terms, respectively. Both phenomena must be taken into account to obtain a comprehensive picture of the illposedness of (1.5) and (1.8) in the presence of a degeneracy in the initial data (and, more concretely, to explain the relevance of the exponents σc\sigma_{c} and scs_{c}).

1. Principal term: dynamics of bicharacteristics. The illposedness of (1.9) from degenerate dispersion can be most easily described at the level of the bicharacteristic ODE system associated with the principal symbol pp of the spatial part of (1.9), which is given by

{X˙=∂ξp⁡(X,Ξ),Ξ˙=−∂xp(X,Ξ),\left\{\begin{aligned} \dot{X}&=\partial_{\xi}p(X,\Xi),\\ \dot{\Xi}&=-\partial_{x}p(X,\Xi),\end{aligned}\right. (1.10)

where p⁡(x,ξ)=−a⁡(x)​ξ2p(x,\xi)=-a(x)\xi^{2} in the Schrödinger case, and −a⁡(x)​ξ3-a(x)\xi^{3} in the KdV case. By geometric optics, the trajectory (X⁡(t),Ξ⁡(t))(X(t),\Xi(t)) describes (at least on sufficiently short timescales) wave packets concentrated near X⁡(t)X(t) in the physical space and Ξ⁡(t)\Xi(t) in the frequency space; see (1.3) and (1.3) below for further discussion. If (1.10) admits the growth of |Ξ||\Xi| by a definite factor (e.g., 22) in arbitrarily short timescales, we would have a strong indication of illposedness of (1.9) in high-regularity Sobolev spaces. In turn, such a growth may come from some degeneracy of pp in XX – this phenomenon is what we shall refer to as degenerate dispersion.

To be concrete, let us assume that dynamics is given in (x,ξ)∈ℝ×ℝ(x,\xi)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R} and the coefficient aa in pp is of the degenerate form a⁡(x)≈A​xna(x)\approx Ax^{n} (n>0)(n>0) for |x||{x}| small, so that

p⁡(x,ξ)≈−A​xn​ξm for |x| small and |ξ| large.\begin{split}p(x,\xi)\approx-Ax^{n}\xi^{m}\quad\hbox{ for $|x|$ small and $|\xi|$ large}.\end{split} (1.11)

Note that m=2m=2 in the Schrödinger case and 33 in the KdV case. The associated bicharacteristic ODE system is

{X˙≈−A​m​Xn​Ξm−1Ξ˙≈A​n​Xn−1​Ξm,\left\{\begin{aligned} \dot{X}&\approx-AmX^{n}\Xi^{m-1}\\ \dot{\Xi}&\approx AnX^{n-1}\Xi^{m},\end{aligned}\right. (1.12)

In view of the fact that the group velocity X˙\dot{X} vanishes at the point x=0x=0 (since n>0n>0), we shall say that pp is degenerate at x=0x=0.

We shall now describe the illposedness mechanism of degenerate dispersion in this concrete case. (This analysis can be found in the introduction of [10] as well.) With a change of the time variable, we may take A=1A=1. Assume, for the sake of this heuristic discussion, that ≈\approx’s above are exact equalities. Consider the solution to (1.12) with initial conditions (X0,Ξ0)(X_{0},\Xi_{0}), where 0<X0≪10<X_{0}\ll 1 and Ξ0≫1\Xi_{0}\gg 1. Then, appealing to the fact that Xn​ΞmX^{n}\Xi^{m} is conserved in time, we have

Ξ⁡(t)=Ξ0​(1+(n−m)​X0n−1​Ξ0m−1​t)mm−n\begin{split}\Xi(t)=\Xi_{0}\left(1+(n-m)X_{0}^{n-1}\Xi_{0}^{m-1}t\right)^{\frac{m}{m-n}}\end{split}

for m≠nm\neq n. When m=nm=n, which will be referred to as the critical case, we have instead

Ξ⁡(t)=Ξ0​exp⁡(m​X0m−1​Ξ0m−1​t).\begin{split}\Xi(t)=\Xi_{0}\exp\left(mX_{0}^{m-1}\Xi_{0}^{m-1}t\right).\end{split} (1.13)

In all cases, the frequency magnitude doubles (i.e., |Ξ⁡(τ2)|=2​|Ξ0||{\Xi(\tau_{2})}|=2|{\Xi_{0}}|) at time τ2≃|Ξ0|1−m​|X0|1−n\tau_{2}\simeq|{\Xi_{0}}|^{1-m}|{X_{0}}|^{1-n}. If the order of pp is greater than 11 (i.e., m>1m>1), the doubling time τ2\tau_{2} may be taken to be arbitrarily small by choosing |Ξ0||{\Xi_{0}}| large, as we desired. Such an arbitrarily fast growth of Ξ\Xi suggests that high derivatives of the solution following this bicharacteristic flow would also grow arbitrarily fast – this is what we shall refer to as illposedness via degenerate dispersion.

Finally, let us connect the above model case to the equations considered in this work. Recall that the principal coefficient aa in the linearized operator is determined by the background solution ff, where a=|f|2a=|{f}|^{2} for (1.5) and a=fa=f for (1.8). Since the relevant frequency doubling time scale τ2\tau_{2} is arbitrarily small, it is reasonable to make the approximation f≈f0f\approx f_{0}. Assuming that f0f_{0} is degenerate at x=0x=0, in the sense that |f0||{f_{0}}| vanishes to some finite order at 00, we arrive at the ansatz a⁡(x)≈A​xna(x)\approx Ax^{n} for some A≠0A\neq 0 and n>0n>0.

Remark 1.10 (Critical degeneracy).

In this work, for simplicity, we shall consider only background solutions with critical degeneracy n=mn=m. The heuristics suggest, however, that a similar arbitrary fast growth of |Ξ||{\Xi}| is expected for any order of degeneracy n>0n>0. The techniques in this paper should be generalizable to these cases.

2. Sub-principal term: evolution of wave packet amplitude and Takeuchi–Mizohata condition. While sub-principal terms do not enter in the dynamics of bicharacteristics, they need to be considered in order to fully understand the well/illposedness issues for (1.9). In fact, the sub-principal term may already cause illposedness in L2L^{2} even when the principal term is nondegenerate! This phenomenon is captured by the classical Takeuchi–Mizohata condition (after the works [34, 24] in the Schrödinger case); see (1.20) below.

To understand this phenomenon, it is instructive to delve a little deeper into the construction of wave packet (approximate) solutions for (1.9). The Takeuchi–Mizohata conditions (cf. [34, 24] in the Schrödinger case; see [1, 4] and Remark 1.12 for the KdV case) are simply sufficient conditions for the forward-in-time boundedness of ‖𝐚‖L2\|{{\bf a}}\|_{L^{2}} read off from (1.19):

supx0<x1|∫x0x1Re⁡b2​a​𝑑x|<+∞\displaystyle\sup_{x_{0}<x_{1}}\left|{\int_{x_{0}}^{x_{1}}\frac{\Re b}{2a}\,\mathrm{d}x}\right|<+\infty  in the Schrödinger case,\displaystyle\quad\hbox{ in the Schr\"{o}dinger case}, (1.20)
supx0<x1∫x0x1b3​a​𝑑x<+∞\displaystyle\sup_{x_{0}<x_{1}}\int_{x_{0}}^{x_{1}}\frac{b}{3a}\,\mathrm{d}x<+\infty  in the KdV case.\displaystyle\quad\hbox{ in the KdV case}. (1.21)

Conversely, the failure of the Takeuchi–Mizohata conditions (1.20), (1.21) signals arbitrarily fast growth (i.e., norm inflation) of the L2L^{2}-norm of uu, since X⁡(t)X(t) may travel arbitrarily far from X0X_{0} in any fixed duration of time if Ξ0\Xi_{0} is large. In this paper, we shall refer to this norm inflation (or illposedness) mechanism as the Takeuchi–Mizohata instability. Below, we shall consider the interaction of degenerate dispersion and the Takeuchi–Mizohata instability, which provides us with a detailed heuristic understanding of the illposedness properties of the linearization of (1.5) and (1.8) in the presence of a (critical) degeneracy in the initial data.

Remark 1.11 (Rigorous results on Takeuchi–Mizohata-type conditions).

The necessity of (1.20) for the L2L^{2}-wellposedness of (1.9) in the Schrödinger case has been known since in the early works [34, 24]; see also [1] for the KdV case. On the other hand, whether such a condition alone is sufficient for L2L^{2} boundedness in general is less clear in general, especially in higher dimensions. Nevertheless, some strengthened form of the Takeuchi–Mizohata condition underlies many works on the wellposedness of the Cauchy problem for linear and even nonlinear Schrödinger- and KdV-type equations; see, e.g., [1, 2, 4, 12, 13, 17, 18, 21, 22, 23, 25].

Remark 1.12 (Role of sgn​b{\mathrm{sgn}}\,b in the KdV case).

Observe that the absolute value is needed in the Schrödinger case (1.20) since X⁡(t)X(t) may travel in both directions, while it is not necessary in the KdV case (1.21) since X⁡(t)X(t) is always decreasing if aa is positive (resp. increasing if aa is negative) according to (1.10). In particular, in the KdV case, (1.21) is always satisfied if b<0b<0, and even when bb has some positive parts, it is possible that the Takeuchi–Mizohata condition is still satisfied (e.g., when bb oscillates). This phenomenon has been explored by Ambrose–Wright [4], who prove wellposedness of some variable coefficient linear KdV-type equations in the periodic setting in the presence of the positive part of bb (referred to as “anti-diffusion” in that paper).

Remark 1.13.

While our main focus is the interaction of Takeuchi–Mizohota instability with degenerate dispersion, the method developed in this paper also provides a new and effective way to rigorously establish the necessity of (1.20) and (1.21) for the L2L^{2}-wellposedness of (1.9). We refer the reader to Section 1.5 and Appendix A below for sample results in the Schrödinger case for a=1a=1 (but in arbitrarily dimensions).

3. Combined effect of degenerate dispersion and Takeuchi–Mizohata instability. We are now ready to discuss the combined effect of the principal and sub-principal terms in (1.9) obtained by linearizing around a background solution ff with a degeneracy. Keeping Remarks 1.9 and 1.10 in mind, we consider the linearization of (1.5) and (1.8) around f⁡(t,x)=xf(t,x)=x and x3x^{3} (for |x||{x}| small), respectively. Then we arrive at (1.9) with

a⁡(x)=x2,b⁡(x)=3​(α12+β1−1)​x\displaystyle a(x)=x^{2},\quad b(x)=3(\tfrac{\alpha_{1}}{2}+\beta_{1}-1)x in the Schrödinger case,\displaystyle\hbox{ in the Schr\"{o}dinger case},

The relevant Takeuchi–Mizohata condition (see (1.22) below with σ=0\sigma=0) for ‖u‖L2\|{u}\|_{L^{2}} may or may not hold, meaning that degenerating wave packets may or may not remain bounded in L2L^{2}. which fails exactly when σ>σc\sigma>\sigma_{c} in both cases. Moreover, the preceding heuristic analysis suggests that the HσH^{\sigma} norm of the degenerating wave packet grows if σ>σc\sigma>\sigma_{c}, stays constant if σ=σc\sigma=\sigma_{c} and decays if σ<σc\sigma<\sigma_{c}. This consideration explains the relevance of the exponent σc\sigma_{c}.

1.4 Discussion of the proof

Our discussion so far has been rather formal; deriving actual nonlinear illposedness in standard function spaces requires more ideas. Our main technical contribution in this work is developing a robust scheme for establishing quantitative illposedness, which is not only able to deduce strong illposedness in quasilinear cases but also yields much stronger statements for linear equations. The scheme largely consists of three parts: 1. construction of degenerating wave packets for the linearized equation, 2. duality testing argument and 3. incorporation of the nonlinearity.

1. Degenerating wave packets. We first describe the ideas for construction of a degenerating wave packet. Compared to the heuristic discussion above, the actual construction of such an approximate solution u~\widetilde{u} to (1.9) has to (1) allow for time-dependent coefficients a=a⁡(t,x)a=a(t,x) and b=b⁡(t,x)b=b(t,x) (as the background solution may depend on time, see Part 3 below), and (2) solve the linearized equation up to an equation error ϵu~\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\widetilde{u}} of size 𝒪⁡(Ξ0m−1−δ)\mathcal{O}(\Xi_{0}^{m-1-\delta}) (in a suitable norm) for some δ>0\delta>0 (here, m=2m=2 for Schrödinger and 33 for KdV). Property (2) is necessary to justify the approximation on a longer time scale than Ξ01−m\Xi_{0}^{1-m}, which is the instability time scale; see (1.13).

Our idea is to make appropriate changes of the independent and dependent variables from (x,u)(x,u) to (y,v)(y,v) to reduce the problem to the constant coefficient case, for which the construction is standard. For time-dependent coefficients a=a⁡(t,x)a=a(t,x) and b=b⁡(t,x)b=b(t,x), the transformation (x,u)↦(y,vˇ)(x,u)\mapsto(y,\check{v}) is of the form

d​x=(a⁡(t,x))1m​d​y,u=(w​wˇ)−1​vˇ, where ​w−1​∂xw=Re⁡bm​a,wˇ−1​∂xwˇ=∂xa2​m​a.\mathrm{d}x=(a(t,x))^{\frac{1}{m}}\mathrm{d}y,\quad u=(w\check{w})^{-1}\check{v},\quad\hbox{ where }w^{-1}\partial_{x}w=\frac{\Re b}{ma},\,\check{w}^{-1}\partial_{x}\check{w}=\frac{\partial_{x}a}{2ma}.

Roughly speaking, Takeuchi–Mizohata instability is renormalized by the conjugation of the dependent variable by the weight ww, in the sense that v⁡(t,x):=w​u​(t,x)v(t,x):=wu(t,x) solves (1.9) with b=0b=0 (with possibly different lower order terms). Similarly, degenerate dispersion is renormalized by the change of variables x↦yx\mapsto y accompanied with the conjugation of the dependent variable by the weight wˇ\check{w}, in the sense that the vˇ​(t,y)\check{v}(t,y) solves the constant coefficient problem (∂t+i(i∂y)m)vˇ=(lower order terms)(\partial_{t}+i(i\partial_{y})^{m})\check{v}=(\hbox{lower order terms}). Now, starting from a standard wave packet for the constant coefficient problem traveling towards the degeneracy and returning to original variables, we obtain a degenerating wave packet u~\widetilde{u} with the desired properties.

In order to make the above heuristic discussion precise, there are several more factors to consider. For instance, we need to make sure that the contribution of ∂ta\partial_{t}a, ∂tb\partial_{t}b are indeed acceptable, which ultimately relies on the estimates we have on the time derivative of the background solution f⁡(t,x)f(t,x) in applications; see 3. below. In the Schrödinger case, we need the following two additional ideas: (i) an extra change of dependent variables to treat terms of the form b~​∂xu¯\widetilde{b}\partial_{x}\overline{u}, and (ii) an extra phase rotation ei​λ​Se^{i\lambda S} for the wave packet vˇ\check{v} to treat terms of the form −(Imb+∂ty)∂yvˇ-(\Im b+\partial_{t}y)\partial_{y}\check{v}, both of which are potentially problematic for achieving Property (2). For more details, see the proofs of Propositions 2.7 and 3.3 for details.

Remark 1.14 (Numerologies in the Schrödinger vs. KdV cases).

In order to justify the properties of u~\widetilde{u} needed for the proof of the HsH^{s}- or CsC^{s}-norm growth, (ii) above forces the technical restriction that f∈Cs+1,1f\in C^{s+1,1} with s≥2s\geq 2 in the Schrödinger case, while f∈Cs−1,1f\in C^{s-1,1} with s≥4s\geq 4 is sufficient in the KdV case; compare the degeneration bounds in Propositions 2.7 and 3.3. This point explains the different numerologies in Theorems 1.1 and 1.2 in the Schrödinger case versus Theorems 1.4 and 1.5 in the KdV case.

2. Modified energy estimate and duality testing argument. In order to upgrade the norm growth for a degenerating wave packet u~\widetilde{u} to an actual solution uu to (1.9), we adapt the energy estimate and duality method introduced in our previous work [16] on Hall–MHD. Here we shall briefly explain the argument, in the simplest setup.

Given a degenerating wave packet u~\widetilde{u} for (1.9), denote by uu any33 3 Note that it is a-priori possible that uniqueness of the Cauchy problem for (1.9) fails. Nevertheless, the method is still applicable and establishes the norm growth of every solution uu with the same initial data satisfying (1.23). solution to (1.9) with u⁡(t=0)=u~0u(t=0)=\widetilde{u}_{0}, where u~0:=u~​(t=0)\widetilde{u}_{0}:=\widetilde{u}(t=0). In view of the aforementioned fact that v=w​uv=wu solves (1.9) with b=0b=0, the following modified energy estimates should hold (at least when uu is sufficiently regular):

∥wu∥Lt∞​([0,t0],L2)≲∥wu0∥L2,∥wu~∥Lt∞​([0,t0],L2)≲∥wu~0∥L2,\begin{split}\|{wu}\|_{L^{\infty}_{t}([0,t_{0}];L^{2})}\lesssim\|{wu_{0}}\|_{L^{2}},\qquad\|{w\widetilde{u}}\|_{L^{\infty}_{t}([0,t_{0}];L^{2})}\lesssim\|{w\widetilde{u}_{0}}\|_{L^{2}},\end{split} (1.23)

where 0<t0<10<t_{0}<1. By the same token, the following generalized (bilinear) energy estimate should also hold:

|dd​t​⟨w​u,w​u~⟩|≲‖w​ϵu‖L2​‖w​u~‖L2+‖w​u‖L2​‖w​ϵu~‖L2.\displaystyle\left|\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\langle{wu,w\widetilde{u}}\rangle\right|\lesssim\|{w\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{u}}\|_{L^{2}}\|{w\widetilde{u}}\|_{L^{2}}+\|{wu}\|_{L^{2}}\|{w\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\widetilde{u}}}\|_{L^{2}}.

(We remark that ∂tw\partial_{t}w also arises, but in applications we shall have |∂tw|≲w|{\partial_{t}w}|\lesssim w.) Here, ϵu\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{u} and ϵu~\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\widetilde{u}} are the errors associated with uu and u~\widetilde{u} viewed as approximate solutions to (1.9). Then, as long as the error terms are bounded, we may deduce that ⟨w​u,w​u~⟩≃⟨w​u0,w​u~0⟩=‖w​u~0‖L22\langle{wu,w\widetilde{u}}\rangle\simeq\langle{wu_{0},w\widetilde{u}_{0}}\rangle=\|{w\widetilde{u}_{0}}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}, which allows us to obtain behavior of uu in various norms by simply estimating the degenerating wave packet u~\widetilde{u} and using duality.

In actual applications, the errors often contain derivatives and hence ‖w​ϵu~‖L2\|{w\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\widetilde{u}}}\|_{L^{2}} (resp. ‖w​ϵu‖L2\|{w\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{u}}\|_{L^{2}}) may diverge as |Ξ0|→∞|\Xi_{0}|\to\infty. Nevertheless, in view of the fact the instability time-scale is ≃|Ξ0|1−m\simeq|{\Xi_{0}}|^{1-m}, for the above argument to work it suffices to have ∫0t0‖w​ϵu~‖L2≲1\int_{0}^{t_{0}}\|{w\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{\widetilde{u}}}\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim 1 (resp. ∫0t0‖w​ϵu‖L2≲1\int_{0}^{t_{0}}\|{w\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{u}}\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim 1) for t0>|Ξ0|1−m+δt_{0}>|{\Xi_{0}}|^{1-m+\delta}. For u~\widetilde{u}, this is precisely Property (2) in the preceding discussion. For an actual solution uu to (1.9), this follows from the fact that ϵu\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{u} does not contain principal nor sub-principal terms (except b~​∂xu¯\widetilde{b}\partial_{x}\overline{u} in the Schrödinger case, which may be integrated by parts away).

3. Incorporation of the nonlinearity. The ideas discussed so far explain how to prove the illposedness of (1.9) that arises from linearizing (1.5) and (1.8) around a regular solution f⁡(t,x)f(t,x) whose initial data has a critical degeneracy at x=0x=0. As in [16], the nonlinear norminflation results (Theorems 1.1 and 1.4) is derived by assuming the existence of a nonlinear perturbation uu around ff (i.e., f+uf+u solves the nonlinear equation) without the instability behavior, then applying the above argument. Moreover, the nonlinear non-existence results (Theorems 1.2 and 1.5) are proved by superposition of infinitely many configurations exhibiting norm inflation (with unbounded rates of growth), with disjoint supports in physical space. We refer to [16, Section 1.6] for a more detailed summary of the ideas involved, and to Sections 2.5, 2.6, 3.5 and 3.6 for details. A key new feature of the present paper compared to [16], however, is that the background solution ff need not be stationary solutions, and are given as a part of the contradiction hypothesis in the proof of the non-existence theorems.

1.5 Revisiting L2L^{2}-illposedness à la Takeuchi–Mizohata

In view of the extensive appearance of the Takeuchi–Mizohata instability in this paper, it is perhaps not surprising that our techniques also apply to the original setting considered by Takeuchi and Mizohata of L2L^{2}-illposedness of linear nondegenerate Schrödinger-type equations. In Appendix A, we provide a few results concerning the Takeuchi–Mizohata condition obtained through our approach. In particular, we recover the following result of Mizohata [25, §VII.2]:

Proposition 1.15.

Consider the following linear first-order perturbation of the Schrödinger equation on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}:

i​∂tu+Δ​u+bj​(x)​∂ju=0i\partial_{t}u+\Delta u+b^{j}(x)\partial_{j}u=0 (1.24)

where b∈C1,1​(ℝd)b\in C^{1,1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Suppose that the Takeuchi–Mizohata condition for (1.24) fails, i.e.,

sup{∫0TRebj(x−2sω)ωjds:x∈ℝd,ω∈𝕊d−1,T>0}=+∞.\sup\left\{\int_{0}^{T}\Re b^{j}(x-2s\omega)\omega_{j}\,\mathrm{d}s:x\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\,\omega\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1},\,T>0\right\}=+\infty. (1.25)

Then for any δ>0\delta>0, every solution map L2→Lt∞​([0,δ],L2)L^{2}\to L^{\infty}_{t}([0,\delta];L^{2}) for (1.24), if it exists, is unbounded.

Note that Proposition 1.15 clearly implies the result proved in [25, §VII.2], namely, the impossibility of having a solution map for the inhomogeneous equation

i​∂tu+Δ​u+bj​(x)​∂ju=fi\partial_{t}u+\Delta u+b^{j}(x)\partial_{j}u=f (1.26)

satisfying

‖u‖L∞​([0,δ],L2)≤C0​(‖u0‖L2+‖f‖L1​([0,δ],L2))\|{u}\|_{L^{\infty}([0,\delta];L^{2})}\leq C_{0}\left(\|{u_{0}}\|_{L^{2}}+\|{f}\|_{L^{1}([0,\delta];L^{2})}\right)

for some C0<+∞C_{0}<+\infty. In fact, via Duhamel’s principle, this result is equivalent to Proposition 1.15. Nonetheless, our techniques generalize easily to other situations when such an equivalence is not obvious, e.g., when bb depends on time.

More interestingly, we also provide some new unconditional quantitative lower bounds for (1.24), which are valid way past the trivial O⁡(1λ)O(\tfrac{1}{\lambda}) time scale (where λ\lambda is the initial characteristic frequency), up to a time when the L2L^{2}-norm may grow at a quantitative rate depending on λ\lambda; see Propositions A.1 and A.3 below. These results should be contrasted with the proofs of Proposition 1.15 and [25, §VII.2] rely on qualitative contradiction arguments up to O⁡(1λ)O(\frac{1}{\lambda}) time scales.

1.6 Organization of the paper

The Schrödinger and KdV-type equations are treated respectively in Sections 2 and 3. In Appendix A, we prove Proposition 1.15 and related results for the linear nondegenerate Schrödinger-type equation (1.24).

2 Schrödinger-type equations

This section is organized as follows. To motivate our approach, we analyze in Section 2.1 a model problem (2.2) derived from (1.1). In Section 2.2, we study the properties of linearly degenerate solutions – typically denoted by ff – and in Section 2.3, we construct degenerating wave packets for the linearized equation around ff. In Section 2.4, we establish a modified and generalized (bilinear) energy estimates for the perturbation (solving the nonlinear difference equation) around ff. Finally, in Sections 2.5 and 2.6, we prove Theorems 1.1 and 1.2, respectively.

2.1 Degenerating wave packets for model linear equation

To motivate what is to follow, consider the case (1.1) (i.e., (1.5) with α1=β1=1\alpha_{1}=\beta_{1}=1 and μ1=0\mu_{1}=0), which we recall here for convenience:

i​∂tϕ+∂x(|ϕ|2​∂xϕ)=0.i\partial_{t}\phi+\partial_{x}(|\phi|^{2}\partial_{x}\phi)=0. (1.1)

|⟨|x|12​ℒ​[v],|x|12​v⟩|≤C​‖|x|12​v‖L22,\begin{split}\left|\langle{|x|^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathcal{L}[v],|x|^{\frac{1}{2}}v}\rangle\right|\leq C\|{|x|^{\frac{1}{2}}v}\|_{L^{2}}^{2},\end{split} (2.3)

which suggests that the correct way to measure regularity for solutions of (2.2) is to use |x|12|x|^{\frac{1}{2}}--weighted spaces55 5 As we shall see below, the exponents 22 and 12\frac{1}{2} in x​e2​i​txe^{2it} and |x|12|{x}|^{\frac{1}{2}}, respectively, should be replaced by appropriate constants for (1.5) in general.. Remark 2.4 (Additional ideas in the proof of Theorems 1.1 and 1.2).

For a general equation of the form (1.5), we do not have access to a stationary solution with a linear degeneracy in general (furthermore, we shall also require that f0f_{0} be compactly supported, which rules out x​e2​i​txe^{2it}, too). Hence, we shall carry out the above analysis (degenerating wave packet construction, modified energy estimate and duality) where the background solution ff is merely a regular (most likely) time-dependent solution to (1.5), which has compactly supported initial data f0f_{0} with a linear degeneracy, in place of x​e2​i​txe^{2it}.

Theorem 1.1 is proved by considering a perturbation f+ϕ~f+\widetilde{\phi} of such an ff, and arguing that if f+ϕ~f+\widetilde{\phi} exists as a regular solution (i.e., if we are in the second case in Theorem 1.1), then the above growth mechanism for ϕ~\widetilde{\phi} can be justified. To prove Theorem 1.2, we consider initial data ϕ~0\widetilde{\phi}_{0} consisting of a superposition of an infinitude of configurations as above (i.e., ∑k(fk,0+ϕ~k,0)\sum_{k}(f_{k,0}+\widetilde{\phi}_{k,0}), where fk,0f_{k,0} has a linear degeneracy and ϕ~k,0\widetilde{\phi}_{k,0} is a degenerating wave packet adapted to fk,0f_{k,0}) with unbounded rates (i.e., the initial frequencies of the degenerating wave packets are unbounded), disjoint supports (i.e., {supp​fk,0∪supp​ϕk,0}k\{{\mathrm{supp}}\,f_{k,0}\cup{\mathrm{supp}}\,\phi_{k,0}\}_{k} is pairwise disjoint), yet with an ϵ\epsilon-small Cm0C^{m_{0}}-norm. Then we perform a contradiction argument: if a regular solution ϕ\phi to such initial data exists, then we may justify the growth mechanism (as in Proposition 2.1), which is absurd. For details, see Sections 2.5 and 2.6 below.

2.3 Degenerating wave packets for the linearized equation

In this subsection, our goal is to construct approximate solutions, called degenerating wave packets, for the linearization of (1.5) around a (possibly hypothetical) regular linearly degenerate solution, which possess the desired degeneration property that is responsible for the illposedness of (1.5); see Proposition 2.7 below.

The above proposition motivates us to define the following hermitian product and norm (which will be referred to as the modified energy): given some ff, we shall consider

‖∂xscϕ~k‖L∞​(t=δk)≳2−N1​k2​|λk|sc​exp⁡(2​|λk|12​(−σc+sc+12)−|λk|14).\begin{split}\|{\partial_{x}^{s_{c}}\tilde{\phi}_{k}}\|_{L^{\infty}}(t=\delta_{k})\gtrsim 2^{-N_{1}k^{2}}|\lambda_{k}|^{s_{c}}\exp\left(2|\lambda_{k}|^{\frac{1}{2}}(-\sigma_{c}+s_{c}+\frac{1}{2})-|\lambda_{k}|^{\frac{1}{4}}\right).\end{split}

Note that the left hand side is bounded by ‖f‖L∞​([0,δ′],Csc+1,1)+‖ϕ‖L∞​([0,δ′],Csc+1,1)\|{f}\|_{L^{\infty}([0,\delta^{\prime}];C^{s_{c}+1,1})}+\|{\phi}\|_{L^{\infty}([0,\delta^{\prime}];C^{s_{c}+1,1})} for all kk sufficiently large. This is a contradiction since the right hand side diverges as k→∞k\to\infty. The proof is now complete. ∎

3 KdV-type equations

This section is organized as follows. After setting up some pieces of notation in Section 3.1, we study the properties of regular cubically degenerate solutions – typically denoted by ff – in Section 3.2. Then in Section 3.3, we carry out the key construction of degenerating wave packets for the linearized equation around ff, and in Section 3.4, we establish a modified energy estimate for the perturbation (solving the nonlinear difference equation) around ff. Finally, in Sections 3.5 and 3.6, we prove Theorems 1.4 and 1.5, respectively.

3.1 Preliminaries

We introduce the following quantity defined for a C2,1C^{2,1} function ff on an interval II:

‖f‖Y⁡(I)=‖f−23​∂xf‖L∞​(I)3+‖f−13​∂x​xf‖L∞​(I)32+‖f‖L∞​(I)+‖∂x​x​xf‖L∞​(I).\begin{split}{\|{f}\|_{Y(I)}=\|{f^{-\frac{2}{3}}\partial_{x}f}\|^{3}_{L^{\infty}(I)}+\|{f^{-\frac{1}{3}}\partial_{xx}f}\|_{L^{\infty}(I)}^{\frac{3}{2}}+\|{f}\|_{L^{\infty}(I)}+\|{\partial_{xxx}f}\|_{L^{\infty}(I)}.}\end{split}

We shall write f∈Y⁡(I)f\in{Y(I)} if ‖f‖Y⁡(I)\|{f}\|_{Y(I)} is finite. This quantity is appropriate to handle solutions with degeneracies of order at least 3. For convenience we set

‖f‖C~k,α​(I)=‖f‖Ck,α​(I)+‖f‖Y⁡(I).\begin{split}{\|{f}\|_{\widetilde{C}^{k,\alpha}(I)}=\|{f}\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(I)}+\|{f}\|_{Y(I)}.}\end{split}

For ff depending on time, we say f∈L∞​([0,δ],C~k,α​(I))f\in L^{\infty}([0,\delta];\widetilde{C}^{k,\alpha}(I)) (resp. f∈L∞​([0,δ];Y⁡(I)CLOSEf\in L^{\infty}([0,\delta];Y(I)) if

‖f‖L∞​([0,δ],C~k,α​(I)):=supt∈[0,δ]‖f⁡(t)‖C~k,α​(I)<+∞.(resp. ∥f∥L∞​([0,δ],Y⁡(I)):=supt∈[0,δ]∥f(t)∥Y⁡(I)<+∞.)\begin{split}\|{f}\|_{L^{\infty}([0,\delta];\widetilde{C}^{k,\alpha}(I))}:=\sup_{t\in[0,\delta]}\|{f(t)}\|_{\widetilde{C}^{k,\alpha}(I)}<+\infty.\\ {(\hbox{resp.~}\|{f}\|_{L^{\infty}([0,\delta];Y(I))}:=\sup_{t\in[0,\delta]}\|{f(t)}\|_{Y(I)}<+\infty.)}\end{split}

It is easy to see using the Taylor expansion, that any C3,αC^{3,\alpha} function which vanishes cubically at its zeroes must belong to YY. However, propagation of YY–boundedness for (1.8) in general requires higher regularity, e.g. C4,1C^{4,1} (see Proposition 3.2).

For later use, we introduce the notation

⟨a,b⟩f(t)=∫f(t,x)−23​σca(t,x)b(t,x)dx,∥a∥Lf2(t)=⟨a,a⟩f​(t).\begin{split}\langle{a,b}\rangle_{f}(t)=\int f(t,x)^{-\frac{2}{3}\sigma_{c}}a(t,x)b(t,x)\,\mathrm{d}x,\quad\|{a}\|_{L^{2}_{f}}(t)=\sqrt{\langle{a,a}\rangle_{f}(t)}.\end{split} (3.1)

For the motivation behind the power f−23​σcf^{-\frac{2}{3}\sigma_{c}}, see Section 3.4.

3.2 Properties of a regular cubically degenerate solution

We first discuss a few basic properties of a regular cubically degenerate solution ff to (1.8), which shall serve as the background for our illposedness mechanism.

Under the assumption f∈Lt∞​C~3,α​(I)f\in L^{\infty}_{t}\widetilde{C}^{3,\alpha}(I) with any α>0\alpha>0, we can propagate the information that ff vanishes cubically on an endpoint of II and compute the coefficient.

Let f∈L∞​([0,δ],C~3,α​(I))f\in L^{\infty}([0,\delta];\widetilde{C}^{3,\alpha}(I)) be a solution of (1.8) with initial data f0f_{0} that is positive on I∖∂II\setminus\partial I and vanishes to order at least 33 on each point in ∂I\partial I, where 0<α≤10<\alpha\leq 1.     where β⁡(t)\beta(t) is the solution of

    β˙(t)=−(2+6α1)β4(t),6β3(0)=f0,x​x​x(a),\begin{split}\dot{\beta}(t)=-{(2+6\alpha_{1})}\beta^{4}(t),\quad 6\beta^{3}(0)=f_{0,xxx}(a),\end{split} (3.3)

    and the implicit constant in O⁡(⋅)O(\cdot) is universal. The same statement applies to b∈∂Ib\in\partial I.

Since we are assuming that f⁡(t,⋅)∈C3f(t,\cdot)\in C^{3}, from (1.8), we have

|∂tf|≤C⁡(|fx​x​x​‖f​|+|fx|​|fx​x|+|​fx‖​f|m−1).\begin{split}|\partial_{t}f|\leq C{(|f_{xxx}||f|+|f_{x}||f_{xx}|+|{f_{x}}||{f}|^{m-1})}.\end{split}

3.3 Degenerating wave packets for the linearized equation

In this subsection, our goal is to construct degenerating wave packets for the linearization of (1.8) around a (possibly hypothetical) regular cubic degenerate solution; see Proposition 3.3 below.

Appendix A Takeuchi–Mizohata illposedness via duality

In this appendix, we show how application of the duality (or generalized energy) argument from [16] and this paper leads to simple proofs of quantitative illposedness results for first-order perturbations of the free Schrödinger equation related to the Takeuchi–Mizohata condition, including Proposition 1.15 (see Appendix A.2).

A.1 One-dimensional case

We begin with the one-dimensional first-order perturbation of the free Schrödinger equation,

i​∂tu+∂x​xu+b⁡(x)​∂xu=0.i\partial_{t}u+\partial_{xx}u+b(x)\partial_{x}u=0. (A.1)

w⁡(x)=exp⁡(∫0xRe⁡b⁡(x′)2​d​x′)w(x)=\exp\left(\int_{0}^{x}\Re\frac{b(x^{\prime})}{2}\,\mathrm{d}x^{\prime}\right)

and the growth factor

M(T,μ)=inf(y,y0):|y|≤μ−1,|y0|≤μ−1exp(∫x0+y0x0+2​T+yReb⁡(x′)2dx′).M(T,\mu)=\inf_{(y,y_{0}):|{y}|\leq\mu^{-1},|{y_{0}}|\leq\mu^{-1}}\exp\left(\int_{x_{0}+y_{0}}^{x_{0}+2T+y}\Re\frac{b(x^{\prime})}{2}\,\mathrm{d}x^{\prime}\right).

Fix also ψ1∈C∞​(ℝ)\psi_{1}\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}) with supp​ψ1⊆{x:|x|<1}{\mathrm{supp}}\,\psi_{1}\subseteq\{x:|{x}|<1\} and ‖ψ1‖L2=1\|{\psi_{1}}\|_{L^{2}}=1. Given μ≥1\mu\geq 1 (inverse spatial scale), define ψμ,x0=μd2​ψ1​(μ⁡(x−x0))\psi_{\mu,x_{0}}=\mu^{\frac{d}{2}}\psi_{1}(\mu(x-x_{0})). Given also λ≥1\lambda\geq 1 (frequency, or inverse semi-classical parameter) – which in practice would be much larger than μ\mu – define

u~(t,x)=w−1(x)ei​λ​x−i​λ2​texp(−∫0λ​tiImb(x−2s)ds)ψμ,x0(x−2λt).\widetilde{u}(t,x)=w^{-1}(x)e^{i\lambda x-i\lambda^{2}t}\exp\left(-\int_{0}^{\lambda t}i\Im b(x-2s)\,\mathrm{d}s\right)\psi_{\mu,x_{0}}(x-2\lambda t). (A.2)

∂x​xv~=−(λ−∫0λ​tIm⁡bx​(x−2​s)​𝑑s)2​v~+2​(i​λ−∫0λ​ti​Im⁡bx​(x−2​s)​𝑑s)​v~​ψx​(x−2​λ​t)ψ⁡(x−2​λ​t)−v~∫0λ​tiImbx​x(x−2s)ds+v~ψx​x​(x−2​λ​t)ψ⁡(x−2​λ​t).\begin{split}\partial_{xx}\widetilde{v}&=-\left(\lambda-\int_{0}^{\lambda t}\Im\,b_{x}(x-2s)\,\mathrm{d}s\right)^{2}\widetilde{v}+2\left(i\lambda-\int_{0}^{\lambda t}i\Im\,b_{x}(x-2s)\,\mathrm{d}s\right)\widetilde{v}\frac{\psi_{x}(x-2\lambda t)}{\psi(x-2\lambda t)}\\ &\quad-\widetilde{v}\int_{0}^{\lambda t}i\Im\,b_{xx}(x-2s)\,\mathrm{d}s+\widetilde{v}\frac{\psi_{xx}(x-2\lambda t)}{\psi(x-2\lambda t)}.\end{split}

(i∂t+ℒ~)v~=λ⁡(Im⁡b⁡(x−2​λ​t)−Im⁡b⁡(x)+2​∫0λ​tIm⁡bx​(x−2​s)​ds)​v~−Imb(−∫0λ​tiImbx(x−2s)ds+ψx​(x−2​λ​t)ψ⁡(x−2​λ​t))v~+(∫0λ​tiImbx(x−2s)ds)2v~+2(−∫0λ​tiImbx(x−2s)ds)v~ψx​(x−2​λ​t)ψ⁡(x−2​λ​t)+(−∫0λ​tiImbx​x(x−2s)ds)v~+ψx​x​(x−2​λ​t)ψ⁡(x−2​λ​t)v~+i2Imbxv~.\begin{split}(i\partial_{t}+\widetilde{\mathcal{L}})\widetilde{v}&=\lambda\left(\Im\,b(x-2\lambda t)-\Im\,b(x)+2\int_{0}^{\lambda t}\Im\,b_{x}(x-2s)\,\mathrm{d}s\right)\widetilde{v}\\ &\quad-\Im\,b\left(-\int_{0}^{\lambda t}i\Im\,b_{x}(x-2s)\,\mathrm{d}s+\frac{\psi_{x}(x-2\lambda t)}{\psi(x-2\lambda t)}\right)\widetilde{v}+\left(\int_{0}^{\lambda t}i\Im\,b_{x}(x-2s)\,\mathrm{d}s\right)^{2}\widetilde{v}\\ &\quad+2\left(-\int_{0}^{\lambda t}i\Im\,b_{x}(x-2s)\,\mathrm{d}s\right)\widetilde{v}\frac{\psi_{x}(x-2\lambda t)}{\psi(x-2\lambda t)}\\ &\quad+\left(-\int_{0}^{\lambda t}i\Im\,b_{xx}(x-2s)\,\mathrm{d}s\right)\widetilde{v}+\frac{\psi_{xx}(x-2\lambda t)}{\psi(x-2\lambda t)}\widetilde{v}+\frac{i}{2}\Im\,b_{x}\,\widetilde{v}.\end{split}

Using

∫0λ​tIm⁡bx​(x−2​s)​ds=−12​Im⁡(b⁡(x−2​λ​t)−b⁡(x))\begin{split}\int_{0}^{\lambda t}\Im\,b_{x}(x-2s)\,\mathrm{d}s=-\frac{1}{2}\Im\left(b(x-2\lambda t)-b(x)\right)\end{split}

we get a cancellation of remaining terms of order λ\lambda. Moreover, the same identity eliminates all integrals on the domain [0,λ​t][0,\lambda t]. Using μ≥1\mu\geq 1 to bound all the other terms by O⁡(μ2)O(\mu^{2}), the proof is complete. ∎

A.2 Multi-dimensional case

We consider the following equation on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}:

i​∂tu+Δ​u+bj​(x)​∂ju=0.i\partial_{t}u+\Delta u+b^{j}(x)\partial_{j}u=0. (A.10)

Unfortunately, the proof of a pointwise lower bound in Proposition A.1 breaks down due to the lack of a simple physical space conjugation that removes Rebj(x)∂j\Re b^{j}(x)\partial_{j}. Instead, we shall prove two (conceptually) weaker statements using the duality method, including Proposition 1.15.

The first result is an unconditional integrated lower bound that is valid for nontrivally long (i.e., t≫λ−1t\gg\lambda^{-1}) timescales. To state this result, given x0∈ℝdx_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, ω0∈𝕊d−1\omega_{0}\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}, μ≥1\mu\geq 1 and T>0T>0, define

Mx0,ω0(T,μ)=infy:|y|≤μ−1exp(−∫0TRebj(x0+y−2sω0)(ω0)jds).M_{x_{0},\omega_{0}}(T,\mu)=\inf_{y:|{y}|\leq\mu^{-1}}\exp\left(-\int_{0}^{T}\Re b^{j}(x_{0}+y-2s\omega_{0})(\omega_{0})_{j}\,\mathrm{d}s\right).

Fix ψ1∈C∞​(ℝd)\psi_{1}\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) with supp​ψ1⊆{x:|x|<1}{\mathrm{supp}}\,\psi_{1}\subseteq\{x:|{x}|<1\} and ‖ψ1‖L2=1\|{\psi_{1}}\|_{L^{2}}=1. Given μ≥1\mu\geq 1, define ψμ,x0=μd2​ψ1​(μ⁡(x−x0))\psi_{\mu,x_{0}}=\mu^{\frac{d}{2}}\psi_{1}(\mu(x-x_{0})). Given also λ≥1\lambda\geq 1, define (cf. [25, §VII.2])

u~(t,x)=ei​λ​ω0⋅x−i​λ2​texp(−∫0λ​tbj(x−2sω0)(ω0)jds)ψμ,x0(x−2λω0t).\widetilde{u}(t,x)=e^{i\lambda\omega_{0}\cdot x-i\lambda^{2}t}\exp\left(-\int_{0}^{\lambda t}b^{j}(x-2s\omega_{0})(\omega_{0})_{j}\mathrm{d}s\right)\psi_{\mu,x_{0}}(x-2\lambda\omega_{0}t).
Proposition A.3.

Let u∈Lt∞​([0,tf],L2)u\in L^{\infty}_{t}([0,t_{f}];L^{2}) be a solution to (A.10) with initial data u0u_{0} satisfying ⟨u0,u~​(0)⟩=1\langle{u_{0},\widetilde{u}(0)}\rangle=1, where u~\widetilde{u} is determined from μ\mu, ν\nu and ψ1\psi_{1} as above. Then as long as

μ≤c​λ13,tf≤c​λ−23,\mu\leq c\lambda^{\frac{1}{3}},\quad t_{f}\leq c\lambda^{-\frac{2}{3}}, (A.11)

where cc is a constant depending only on ‖b‖C1,1\|{b}\|_{C^{1,1}} and ‖ψ1‖H2\|{\psi_{1}}\|_{H^{2}}, u⁡(t)u(t) necessarily satisfies the averaged lower bound

1tf​∫0tf(1+μ−1​λ​t)2(1+μ−1​λ​tf)2​Mx0,ω0​(λ​t,μ)−1​‖u⁡(t)‖L2​𝑑t≥16​‖u0‖L2.\frac{1}{t_{f}}\int_{0}^{t_{f}}\frac{(1+\mu^{-1}\lambda t)^{2}}{(1+\mu^{-1}\lambda t_{f})^{2}}M_{x_{0},\omega_{0}}(\lambda t,\mu)^{-1}\|{u(t)}\|_{L^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}t\geq\frac{1}{6}\|{u_{0}}\|_{L^{2}}. (A.12)

An example of an initial data u0u_{0} satisfying the above hypothesis is, of course, u0=u~​(0)u_{0}=\widetilde{u}(0), in which case uu is expected to behave like u~\widetilde{u}. An argument similar to the proof of (A.14) shows that

∥u~(t)∥L2≤supy:|y|≤μ−1exp(−∫0λ​tRebj(x0+y−2sω0)(ω0)jds)∥u~(0)∥L2.\|{\widetilde{u}(t)}\|_{L^{2}}\leq\sup_{y:|{y}|\leq\mu^{-1}}\exp\left(-\int_{0}^{\lambda t}\Re b^{j}(x_{0}+y-2s\omega_{0})(\omega_{0})_{j}\,\mathrm{d}s\right)\|{\widetilde{u}(0)}\|_{L^{2}}.

Thence, provided we choose μ−1\mu^{-1} to be sufficiently small depending on bb, (A.12) is sharp for u~\widetilde{u} up to a constant.

Proof.

We introduce ℒ\mathcal{L} and its formal L2L^{2}-adjoint ℒ∗\mathcal{L}^{\ast} (in operator notation),

ℒ=Δ+bj(x)∂j,ℒ∗=Δ−∂jb¯j(x).\mathcal{L}=\Delta+b^{j}(x)\partial_{j},\quad\mathcal{L}^{\ast}=\Delta-\partial_{j}\overline{b}^{j}(x).

The basis of the proof of Proposition A.3 is the following generalized energy identity:

dd​t⟨u1,u2⟩=−⟨(i∂t+ℒ)u1,iu2⟩−⟨iu1,(i∂t+ℒ∗)u2⟩,\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\langle{u_{1},u_{2}}\rangle=-\langle{(i\partial_{t}+\mathcal{L})u_{1},iu_{2}}\rangle-\langle{iu_{1},(i\partial_{t}+\mathcal{L}^{\ast})u_{2}}\rangle, (A.13)

which is a consequence of the Leibniz rule for ∂t\partial_{t} and 0=⟨i​ℒ​u1,u2⟩+⟨i​u1,i​ℒ∗​u2⟩0=\langle{i\mathcal{L}u_{1},u_{2}}\rangle+\langle{iu_{1},i\mathcal{L}^{\ast}u_{2}}\rangle. A simple but important observation is that (A.13) holds even under the weak assumption u1=u∈Lt∞​([0,tf],L2)u_{1}=u\in L^{\infty}_{t}([0,t_{f}];L^{2}), provided that u2u_{2} is nice enough, e.g., smooth in t,xt,x and compactly supported in space for each fixed time.

The identity (A.13) motivates us to consider not a wave packet for i∂t+ℒi\partial_{t}+\mathcal{L}, but rather its adjoint i∂t+ℒ∗i\partial_{t}+\mathcal{L}^{\ast}. Given 1≤μ≤λ1\leq\mu\leq\lambda, consider

u~∗​(t,x)=ei​λ​ω0⋅x−i​λ2​t​exp⁡(∫0λ​tb¯j​(x−2​s​ω0)​(ω0)j​𝑑s)​ψμ,x0​(x−2​λ​ω0​t).\widetilde{u}^{\ast}(t,x)=e^{i\lambda\omega_{0}\cdot x-i\lambda^{2}t}\exp\left(\int_{0}^{\lambda t}\overline{b}^{j}(x-2s\omega_{0})(\omega_{0})_{j}\mathrm{d}s\right)\psi_{\mu,x_{0}}(x-2\lambda\omega_{0}t).

Observe that

exp(∫0λ​tReb¯j(x−2sω0)(ω0)jds)≤M(λt,μ)−1 for x∈suppψμ,x0(⋅−2λω0t),\exp\left(\int_{0}^{\lambda t}\Re\overline{b}^{j}(x-2s\omega_{0})(\omega_{0})_{j}\mathrm{d}s\right)\leq M(\lambda t,\mu)^{-1}\quad\hbox{ for }x\in{\mathrm{supp}}\,\psi_{\mu,x_{0}}(\cdot-2\lambda\omega_{0}t),

where we have introduced the abbreviation M⁡(λ​t,μ)=Mx0,ω0​(λ​t,μ)M(\lambda t,\mu)=M_{x_{0},\omega_{0}}(\lambda t,\mu). Hence, using also that Re⁡b¯j=Re⁡bj\Re\overline{b}^{j}=\Re b^{j}, it follows that

‖u~∗​(t)‖L2≤M​(λ​t,μ)−1.\|{\widetilde{u}^{\ast}(t)}\|_{L^{2}}\leq M(\lambda t,\mu)^{-1}. (A.14)

The following lemma quantifies the error ϵ[u~∗]=(i∂t+Δ)u~∗−∂j(b¯j(x)u~∗)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}[\widetilde{u}^{\ast}]=(i\partial_{t}+\Delta)\widetilde{u}^{\ast}-\partial_{j}(\overline{b}^{j}(x)\widetilde{u}^{\ast}) incurred by u~∗\widetilde{u}^{\ast}.

Lemma A.4.

There exists a constant C0C_{0}, which depends only on ‖b‖C1,1\|{b}\|_{C^{1,1}} and ‖ψ1‖H2\|{\psi_{1}}\|_{H^{2}}, such that

‖ϵ⁡[u~∗]​(t)‖L2≤C0​(μ+λ​t)2​M​(λ​t,μ)−1.\|{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}[\widetilde{u}^{\ast}](t)}\|_{L^{2}}\leq C_{0}(\mu+\lambda t)^{2}M(\lambda t,\mu)^{-1}. (A.15)

We are now ready to implement the duality method. Assume for the moment that, for some B>0B>0, we have

1tf​‖(1+μ−1​λ​t)2(1+μ−1​λ​tf)2​M​(λ​t,μ)−1​u‖Lt1​([0,tf],L2)<B​‖u0‖L2.\frac{1}{t_{f}}\left\|{\frac{(1+\mu^{-1}\lambda t)^{2}}{(1+\mu^{-1}\lambda t_{f})^{2}}M(\lambda t,\mu)^{-1}u}\right\|_{L^{1}_{t}([0,t_{f}];L^{2})}<B\|{u_{0}}\|_{L^{2}}. (A.16)

By (A.13) and (A.15), we then have

|dd​t​⟨u,u~∗⟩|≤C0​(μ+λ​t)2​M​(λ​t,μ)−1​‖u⁡(t)‖L2.\left|{\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\langle{u,\widetilde{u}^{\ast}}\rangle}\right|\leq C_{0}(\mu+\lambda t)^{2}M(\lambda t,\mu)^{-1}\|{u(t)}\|_{L^{2}}.

⟨u,u~∗⟩​(t)≥‖v0‖L2​(1−B​C0​μ2​(1+μ−1​λ​tf)2​tf).\langle{u,\widetilde{u}^{\ast}}\rangle(t)\geq\|{v_{0}}\|_{L^{2}}\left(1-BC_{0}\mu^{2}(1+\mu^{-1}\lambda t_{f})^{2}t_{f}\right).

Suppose that

μ≤(18​B​C0)13​λ13,tf≤(18​B​C0)13​λ−23.\mu\leq(\tfrac{1}{8BC_{0}})^{\frac{1}{3}}\lambda^{\frac{1}{3}},\quad t_{f}\leq(\tfrac{1}{8BC_{0}})^{\frac{1}{3}}\lambda^{-\frac{2}{3}}. (A.17)

Dividing into two cases tf≤μλt_{f}\leq\frac{\mu}{\lambda} and tf≥μλt_{f}\geq\frac{\mu}{\lambda}, it follows that

B​C0​μ2​(1+μ−1​λ​tf)2​tf≤12.BC_{0}\mu^{2}(1+\mu^{-1}\lambda t_{f})^{2}t_{f}\leq\frac{1}{2}.

Therefore,

⟨u,u~∗⟩​(t)≥12​‖u0‖L2 for all ​0≤t≤tf.\langle{u,\widetilde{u}^{\ast}}\rangle(t)\geq\frac{1}{2}\|{u_{0}}\|_{L^{2}}\quad\hbox{ for all }0\leq t\leq t_{f}.

Then, applying (A.14), we obtain the lower bound

‖u⁡(t)‖L2≥12​M​(λ​t,μ)​‖u0‖L2.\|{u(t)}\|_{L^{2}}\geq\frac{1}{2}M(\lambda t,\mu)\|{u_{0}}\|_{L^{2}}. (A.18)

We now multiply both sides by (1+μ−1​λ​t)2​M​(λ​t,μ)−1(1+\mu^{-1}\lambda t)^{2}M(\lambda t,\mu)^{-1} and integrate. Since

∫0tf(1+μ−1​λ​t)2​𝑑t≥13​tf​(1+μ−1​λ​tf)2,\int_{0}^{t_{f}}(1+\mu^{-1}\lambda t)^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t\geq\frac{1}{3}t_{f}(1+\mu^{-1}\lambda t_{f})^{2},

we arrive at

1tf​‖(1+μ−1​λ​t)2(1+μ−1​λ​tf)2​M​(λ​t,μ)−1​u‖Lt1​([0,tf],L2)≥16​‖u0‖L2.\frac{1}{t_{f}}\left\|{\frac{(1+\mu^{-1}\lambda t)^{2}}{(1+\mu^{-1}\lambda t_{f})^{2}}M(\lambda t,\mu)^{-1}u}\right\|_{L^{1}_{t}([0,t_{f}];L^{2})}\geq\frac{1}{6}\|{u_{0}}\|_{L^{2}}. (A.19)

To complete the proof, we assume, for the purpose of contradiction, that (A.16) holds with B=16B=\frac{1}{6}. Take c=(34​C0)13c=(\tfrac{3}{4C_{0}})^{\frac{1}{3}} in (A.11) so that (A.17) is satisfied. Then by the preceding argument, we arrive at (A.19), which is a contradiction that establishes (A.10). ∎

Proof of Lemma A.4.

As in the proof of Lemma A.2, we compute with ψ=ψμ,x0\psi=\psi_{\mu,x_{0}} that

i​∂tu~∗=λ2​u~∗+i​λ​b¯j​(x−2​λ​t​ω0)​(ω0)j​u~∗−2​i​λ​ω0⋅∇ψψ​u~∗.\begin{split}i\partial_{t}\widetilde{u}^{\ast}=\lambda^{2}\widetilde{u}^{\ast}+i\lambda\overline{b}^{j}(x-2\lambda t\omega_{0})(\omega_{0})_{j}\widetilde{u}^{\ast}-2i\lambda\frac{\omega_{0}\cdot\nabla\psi}{\psi}\widetilde{u}^{\ast}.\end{split}

Introducing for simplicity

Ik(x)=−∫0λ​t∂kb¯j(x−2sω0)(ω0)jds,I(x)=(I1,⋯,Id),\begin{split}I_{k}(x)=-\int_{0}^{\lambda t}\,\partial_{k}\overline{b}^{j}(x-2s\omega_{0})(\omega_{0})_{j}\,\mathrm{d}s,\qquad I(x)=(I_{1},\cdots,I_{d}),\end{split}

we have

∂ku~∗=(i​λ​(ω0)k−Ik+∂kψψ)​u~∗,Δ​u~∗=−λ2​|ω0|2​u~∗−2​i​λ​ω0⋅I​u~∗+2​i​λ​ω0⋅∇ψψ​u~∗+ℛ⁡[u~∗],\begin{split}\partial_{k}\widetilde{u}^{\ast}&=\left(i\lambda(\omega_{0})_{k}-I_{k}+\frac{\partial_{k}\psi}{\psi}\right)\widetilde{u}^{\ast},\\ \Delta\widetilde{u}^{\ast}&=-\lambda^{2}|\omega_{0}|^{2}\widetilde{u}^{\ast}-2i\lambda\omega_{0}\cdot I\,\widetilde{u}^{\ast}+2i\lambda\frac{\omega_{0}\cdot\nabla\psi}{\psi}\,\widetilde{u}^{\ast}+\mathcal{R}[\widetilde{u}^{\ast}],\end{split}

where

ℛ⁡[u~∗]=(|I|2−2​I⋅∇ψψ+|∇ψ|2ψ2+∑k∂k∂kψψ−∇⋅I)​u~∗.\begin{split}\mathcal{R}[\widetilde{u}^{\ast}]=\left(|I|^{2}-\frac{2I\cdot\nabla\psi}{\psi}+\frac{|\nabla\psi|^{2}}{\psi^{2}}+\sum_{k}\partial_{k}\frac{\partial_{k}\psi}{\psi}-\nabla\cdot I\right)\widetilde{u}^{\ast}.\end{split}

Then, after several direct cancellations, we have

(i∂t+ℒ~)u~∗−∂j(b¯j(x)u~∗)=(−2iλω0⋅I+iλb¯j(x−2λtω0)(ω0)j−iλb¯j(x)(ω0)j)u~∗+ℛ⁡[u~∗]−b¯j​(x)​Ij​(x)​u~∗+b¯j​(x)​∂jψψ​u~∗−(∂jb¯j​(x))​u~∗\begin{split}(i\partial_{t}+\widetilde{\mathcal{L}})\widetilde{u}^{\ast}-\partial_{j}(\overline{b}^{j}(x)\widetilde{u}^{\ast})&=\left(-2i\lambda\omega_{0}\cdot I+i\lambda\overline{b}^{j}(x-2\lambda t\omega_{0})(\omega_{0})_{j}-i\lambda\overline{b}^{j}(x)(\omega_{0})_{j}\right)\widetilde{u}^{\ast}\\ &\qquad+\mathcal{R}[\widetilde{u}^{\ast}]-\overline{b}^{j}(x)I_{j}(x)\widetilde{u}^{\ast}+\frac{\overline{b}^{j}(x)\partial_{j}\psi}{\psi}\widetilde{u}^{\ast}-(\partial_{j}\overline{b}^{j}(x))\widetilde{u}^{\ast}\end{split}

and as in the one-dimensional case, we use that

12​(b¯j​(x−2​λ​t​ω0)−b¯j​(x))=∫0λ​t12​dd​s​b¯j​(x−2​s​ω0)​𝑑s=∑kIk​(x)​(ω0)k\begin{split}\frac{1}{2}\left(\overline{b}^{j}(x-2\lambda t\omega_{0})-\overline{b}^{j}(x)\right)=\int_{0}^{\lambda t}\frac{1}{2}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}s}\overline{b}^{j}(x-2s\omega_{0})\,\mathrm{d}s=\sum_{k}I_{k}(x)(\omega_{0})_{k}\end{split}

to get cancellations among the O⁡(λ)O(\lambda) terms77 7 Unlike the one-dimensional case, however, we cannot eliminate the integral on the domain [0,λ​t][0,\lambda t] in II. Hence, we let the right-hand side of (A.15) depend on λ​t\lambda t.. It is now not difficult to see that the remaining terms are bounded in L2L^{2} by the right hand side of (A.15). ∎

As alluded to before, the second result we shall prove using essentially the same argument is Proposition 1.15, i.e., that the failure of the Takeuchi–Mizohata condition (see (1.25)) implies norm inflation for (A.10).

Proof of Proposition 1.15.

Assume, for contradiction, that there exists B0<+∞B_{0}<+\infty such that, for every u0∈L2u_{0}\in L^{2},

‖u‖L∞​([0,δ],L2)≤B0​‖u0‖L2.\|{u}\|_{L^{\infty}([0,\delta];L^{2})}\leq B_{0}\|{u_{0}}\|_{L^{2}}. (A.20)

By (1.25), there exists a sequence (xn,ωn,Tn)(x_{n},\omega_{n},T_{n}) such that

Mxn,ωn​(Tn):=exp⁡(∫0TnRe⁡bj​(xn−2​s​ωn)​(ωn)j​𝑑x)≥e2​n.M_{x_{n},\omega_{n}}(T_{n}):=\exp\left(\int_{0}^{T_{n}}\Re b^{j}(x_{n}-2s\omega_{n})(\omega_{n})_{j}\,\mathrm{d}x\right)\geq e^{2n}.

By restarting from the point xn+2​T​ωnx_{n}+2T\omega_{n} where Mxn,ωn​(T)=1M_{x_{n},\omega_{n}}(T)=1 if necessary, we may assume also that Mxn,ωn​(T)≥1M_{x_{n},\omega_{n}}(T)\geq 1 for all 0≤T≤Tn0\leq T\leq T_{n}. Since Mxn,ωn​(Tn,μ)→Mxn,ωn​(Tn)M_{x_{n},\omega_{n}}(T_{n},\mu)\to M_{x_{n},\omega_{n}}(T_{n}) as μ→∞\mu\to\infty, we may choose μn\mu_{n} so that

Mxn,ωn​(Tn,μn)≥en.M_{x_{n},\omega_{n}}(T_{n},\mu_{n})\geq e^{n}.

We shall apply the argument in the proof of Proposition A.3 with the parameters

tf=Tnλn,x0=xn,ω0=ωn,μ=μn,λ=λn,t_{f}=\frac{T_{n}}{\lambda_{n}},\quad x_{0}=x_{n},\quad\omega_{0}=\omega_{n},\quad\mu=\mu_{n},\quad\lambda=\lambda_{n},

where λn\lambda_{n} shall be determined below. We denote by u~n∗\widetilde{u}^{\ast}_{n} the wave packet for i∂t+ℒ~∗i\partial_{t}+\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}^{\ast} with these parameters, and unu_{n} the solution to (A.10) with initial data u0=u~n∗​(0)u_{0}=\widetilde{u}^{\ast}_{n}(0) satisfying (A.20). Taking λn\lambda_{n} to be large enough, we may guarantee that tf=Tnλn≤δt_{f}=\frac{T_{n}}{\lambda_{n}}\leq\delta. Then by the contradiction assumption and the bound M⁡(T)≥1M(T)\geq 1, it follows that (A.16) is satisfied for u=unu=u_{n} with B=C1​B0B=C_{1}B_{0}, where C1C_{1} depends only on ‖∂b‖L∞\|{\partial b}\|_{L^{\infty}}. Furthermore, choosing λn\lambda_{n} sufficiently large depending on B0B_{0}, C0C_{0}, C1C_{1} and TnT_{n}, we may ensure that (A.17) holds (here, it is important that the power of λ\lambda in the second inequality is greater than −1-1). Thence, it follows from (A.18) and our choices of parameters that

‖un​(Tnλn)‖L2≥12​en​‖un​(0)‖L2.\|{u_{n}(\tfrac{T_{n}}{\lambda_{n}})}\|_{L^{2}}\geq\frac{1}{2}e^{n}\|{u_{n}(0)}\|_{L^{2}}.

Taking n→∞n\to\infty, we arrive at a contradiction. ∎

Remark A.5.

We note that when d=1d=1, Proposition 1.15 is essentially a consequence of Proposition A.1, although pedantically the notion of solution is slightly different due to the presence of a conjugation when d=1d=1. On the other hand, the preceding proof applies to all d≥1d\geq 1.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
